```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
library(data.table)
A <- "docs/assets/variant_artifacts"
rd <- function(f) fread(file.path(A, f))
cas <- rd("ctwas_cascade_counts.tsv"); pu <- rd("panel_vs_ukb.tsv"); sup <- rd("qtl_support.tsv")
nh <- rd("qtl_nhet.tsv"); ctx <- rd("qtl_context.tsv"); chk <- rd("mapping_checks.tsv")
ab <- rd("het_calls_ab.tsv"); cl <- rd("clusters.tsv"); q05 <- rd("q05_by_support.tsv")
ex <- rd("examples.tsv")
fmt <- function(n) format(n, big.mark=",", trim=TRUE)
qs <- q05[, .(present=sum(`in panel`), absent=sum(`not in panel`))]
panel_n <- sup[support == "in panel", snvs]; absent_n <- sup[support == "not in panel", snvs]
qual_col <- "panel site typed or R2 >= 0.8"
start_counts <- cas[step == "QTL set screen"][order(tp)]
```

# 1. Where cTWAS predictors are lost

We noticed this issue while preparing cTWAS models to connect our splicing
associations with the schizophrenia (SCZ) GWAS. Each predictor uses one SNV
associated with an exonic part, and cTWAS needs that SNV in its LD reference.

We started with the **Screen before FDR** from the
[genome-wide results](isolaser_fdr.html#genome-wide-results). Restricting the
candidate SNVs to the UKB LD reference removed a large fraction of the
associations. At baseline, for example,
`r cas[tp == "0hr" & step == "single-base SNV", associations]` SNV associations
became `r cas[tp == "0hr" & step == "variant in the UKB b38 reference", associations]`.
This prompted us to check the coordinates, compare variants with our panel,
and inspect their sequence context and read patterns.

```{r cascade}
lab <- c(`QTL set screen`="Screen before FDR (same as FDR page)", `single-base SNV`="Single-base SNVs",
         `variant in the UKB b38 reference`="Variant matches UKB LD reference",
         `not strand-ambiguous`="Remove A/T and C/G SNPs", `top QTL per part`="Choose one QTL per exonic part",
         `SNP in the SCZ GWAS (final cTWAS traits)`="Chosen SNP also in SCZ GWAS")
cas[, display := sprintf("%s (%s)", fmt(associations), fmt(genes))]
wide <- dcast(cas, step ~ tp, value.var="display")[match(names(lab), step)]
knitr::kable(wide[, .(Step=lab[step], `0 hr`=`0hr`, `1 hr`=`1hr`, `6 hr`=`6hr`)], align="lrrr")
```

**Cells show associations (genes), matching the convention on the FDR page.**
An association is a gene x variant x exonic part at one timepoint. Several
variants can be associated with the same part. The screen's
`r paste(start_counts$associations, collapse=" / ")` associations therefore
represent `r paste(start_counts$parts, collapse=" / ")` distinct exonic parts
at 0 / 1 / 6 hr.
After choosing one QTL per part, the association counts are also the numbers
of cTWAS predictors.

The UKB LD reference contains variants with minor allele frequency >1% in White
British samples, so genuine rare or filtered variants may be missing.
[Reference documentation](https://xinhe-lab.github.io/multigroup_ctwas/articles/preparing_input_data.html#reference-variants-and-ld-matrices)
One missing SNP can remove several parts.

The coordinate checks support the current conversion: all `r chk$snvs[1]` REF
bases agree with GRCh38, and offsets of -2, -1, +1, and +2 bp yield only
`r sum(chk[offset_bp != 0, snvs_matching_ukb])` allele-matched variant/offset pairs,
compared with `r chk[offset_bp == 0, snvs_matching_ukb]` at the correct positions.

# 2. What distinguishes variants absent from our panel?

"Present in our panel" means our genotype panel has a record at the same
position with the same two alleles. It does **not** establish that any particular
donor is heterozygous.

```{r evidence}
pct <- function(d, group, col) paste0(d[support == group, get(col)], "%")
hn <- nh[set == "q < 0.05"]
evidence <- data.table(
  Measure=c("Distinct screened SNVs", "Associations with q < 0.05",
            "SNVs in homopolymer context", "SNVs within 10 bp of an exon edge",
            "Significant associations with 3-4 eligible RNA donors"),
  `Present in our panel`=c(fmt(panel_n), fmt(qs$present), pct(ctx, "in panel", "homopolymer_ge4"),
                    pct(ctx, "in panel", "exon_edge_le10"), pct(hn, "in panel", "pct_eligible_3_4")),
  `Absent from our panel`=c(fmt(absent_n), fmt(qs$absent), pct(ctx, "not in panel", "homopolymer_ge4"),
                   pct(ctx, "not in panel", "exon_edge_le10"), pct(hn, "not in panel", "pct_eligible_3_4")))
knitr::kable(evidence, align="lrr")
```

**Definitions:** homopolymer context means a run of >=4 identical A/C/G/T bases
containing the SNV or an immediately adjacent base in a 21-base reference window.
Exon distance uses annotated exon boundaries, not each read's actual splice junction.
An eligible RNA donor has >=30 informative reads and alternate fraction 0.25-0.75
for that association. These are RNA-based eligibility counts, not DNA genotypes.
Repeated variants and selection for detectable effects prevent treating the donor
counts as independent population-genotype observations.

As a reference check, `r pu[set == "all panel SNVs", pct_in_ukb]`% of SNVs in our panel
match UKB; the allele-frequency correlation on up to 200,000 shared sites flagged
TYPED is `r pu$af_correlation_with_ukb_eur[1]`. This shows agreement between
datasets, not the ancestry or genotype accuracy of each donor.

# 3. Read-level patterns and concrete examples

Across all PASS heterozygous RNA SNV calls with depth >=10, variants absent from
our panel show a lower alternate-read fraction and more clustering:

![](assets/variant_artifacts/ab_by_cluster.png)

```{r allele-balance}
knitr::kable(ab[, .(Group=sub("in genotype panel", "in our panel", sub("not in panel", "not in our panel", as.character(group), fixed=TRUE), fixed=TRUE), Calls=fmt(calls), Sites=fmt(sites),
                    `Median ALT fraction`=median_ab,
                    `% of row's sites in clusters of >=5`=fifelse(is.na(pct_sites_in_clusters_ge5), "--", as.character(pct_sites_in_clusters_ge5)))], align="lrrrr")
```

RNA allele imbalance can be biological, so departure from 0.5 is a warning sign,
not proof of an error. A cluster contains >=3 sites linked by consecutive gaps
<=1 kb; its total span can exceed 1 kb. Sites are pooled across donors and
timepoints. "Nonclustered" includes single sites and two-site groups.

For example, the RPLP0 cluster contains `r cl[genes == "RPLP0", sites]` sites in
`r cl[genes == "RPLP0", span_bp]` bp, with calls from
`r cl[genes == "RPLP0", donors]` donors. This warrants checking paralog/pseudogene
alignments. It does not mean every site occurs in every donor. Genuine variation
can also cluster, especially in polymorphic regions such as HLA.

```{r examples}
knitr::kable(ex[, .(Gene=gene, `Our panel`=fifelse(in_panel, "Yes", "No"), UKB=fifelse(in_ukb, "Yes", "No"),
                    `Reference sequence (SNV in brackets)`=context,
                    `Exon-edge distance (bp)`=edge_dist)], align="llllr")
```

For **AHI1**, changing the central C to T joins two five-T runs into 11 Ts;
for **WDR45B**, it makes a ten-T run. These contexts and the missing records in our panel
make the calls suspicious, but do not prove C-to-T sequencing errors.
**HNRNPK and KPNA2** have records in our panel and UKB and are better-supported
follow-up candidates. HNRNPK's proximity to an exon boundary does not establish causality.

# 4. Potential causes

These explanations are consistent with the observed patterns, but require
read-level or independent genotype validation.

- **Misalignment to a similar gene:** reads from a paralog or processed
  pseudogene may align to the wrong copy. Differences between the copies can
  appear as several nearby SNVs, recurring across donors.
- **ONT basecalling errors:** difficult sequence contexts, including interrupted
  runs of identical bases such as the AHI1 and WDR45B examples, may produce the
  same error in a fraction of reads. A donor can then appear heterozygous in RNA
  even if its genotype is homozygous.
- **Splice-junction alignment errors:** an incorrectly placed exon boundary can
  create apparent mismatches near the junction. If this occurs preferentially in
  one isoform, it can also create an apparent allele-splicing association.

**Why permutation may still find significance:** if an erroneous base call or
alignment occurs preferentially in one isoform, called allele and splicing status
are associated. Shuffling breaks that association and can produce a small p-value.
The test does not establish that the called allele exists in DNA. These are known
challenges in [long-read RNA variant calling](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13059-023-02923-y).

This approach sacrifices some genuine variants missing from our panel. The current
evidence supports cautious follow-up; the fraction of false variant calls remains unknown.

**Data:** SNVs from the screen (`cis`, absolute delta-PSI >=0.10); associations are
gene x SNV x exonic part x timepoint. QTL results use the recording rerun; the
genome-wide call histogram uses the earlier Nanopore runs from the
[variant-validation page](isolaser_variants.html). Variant IDs are isoLASER 0-based;
VCF/UKB positions add one. Tables and figure are computed by
`8.isolaser_validation/21.variant_artifacts.R`.
